title: bug(hook): auto_reclaim_stale_claims never reaches gc hook --claim, so #6402 reclaim is inert
body:
### Symptom

Setting `auto_reclaim_stale_claims = true` on an agent has no effect. `gc hook --claim` never attempts the stale-lease reclaim that #6402 added, so route-matched work that is still assigned to a stale session is skipped, just as before.

### Root cause

`claimFirstEligibleHookCandidate` reclaims only when `hookClaimOptions.AutoReclaimStaleClaims` is true (`cmd/gc/cmd_hook_claim.go:794`). Those options are built in one production place, `cmd/gc/cmd_hook.go:474-482`. That literal sets `Assignee`, `SessionID`, `IdentityCandidates`, `RouteTargets`, `Env`, `DrainAck` and `JSON`, but not `AutoReclaimStaleClaims`, even though the resolved agent `a` is in scope there.

The setting is parsed and layered (`internal/config/config.go:727`, `:3385`; `internal/config/pack.go:2820`) and deep-copied for pools (`cmd/gc/pool.go:327`). Nothing on the claim path reads it. The #6402 tests set the option directly on `hookClaimOptions`, so they pass anyway.

### Reproduction

On main at ad34febe7:

```sh
git grep -n AutoReclaimStaleClaims -- 'cmd/gc/*.go' ':!*_test.go'
```

This lists only the option's definition and its one read in `cmd_hook_claim.go`, plus the pool deep copy in `pool.go`. `cmd_hook.go` never sets it. I found this while rebasing a downstream fork onto #6402; I have not run it end to end against a live bd lease.

### Proposed fix

1. Set `AutoReclaimStaleClaims: a.AutoReclaimStaleClaims` in the literal at `cmd/gc/cmd_hook.go:474`. Add a test that goes through the command path rather than building `hookClaimOptions` by hand, and asserts that the reclaim is attempted.
2. Alternatively, resolve the setting inside `claimHookWork` from the agent config, so no future caller that builds claim options can miss it.

One thing to weigh when it is wired: the reclaim decides staleness from bd's lease TTL alone. A lease can lapse while the session recorded in `gc.session_id` is still working in the bead's worktree. Downstream, we saw two live sessions in one worktree from a similar reclaim, so checking that session's liveness before the reclaim may be worth it.

### Environment

gastownhall/gascity main at ad34febe7 (2026-09-17). The defect is visible by reading the code on any platform.

title: bug(controller): order-tracking retention runs before the city reports ready
body:
### Symptom

After a supervisor restart, the synchronous order-tracking retention pass can delay city readiness. This happens when the store is slow or holds a large closed order-tracking set. Until readiness is published, city-scoped API requests return 404 ("city not found or not running").

We saw about six minutes of this on a city with ~73k closed tracking beads on a slow Dolt server:

```
gc start: ≥1001 closed order-tracking beads detected — retention watchdog will prune automatically (7d TTL default; ...)
startup watchdog: city "westeros" not ready after 2m30s (half of [daemon].start_ready_timeout=5m0s); goroutine dump follows
```

In the goroutine dump, the tick goroutine was inside the sweep:

```
CityRuntime.run -> safeTick -> dispatchOrders -> runOrderTrackingRetentionWatchdog
  -> sweepClosedOrderTrackingRetentionAcrossStoresBounded -> ... -> deleteWorkflowBead -> ... -> List
```

That run was on a build of our fork. The ordering described below is the same on main, and the test below reproduces the defect there.

### Root cause

`run()` dispatches orders in a pre-readiness step, `startup-orders` (`cmd/gc/city_runtime.go:663-667`). It publishes readiness through `onStarted` only after that (`:781-783`). `markReady` at `:784` stops the startup watchdog.

`dispatchOrders` calls `runOrderTrackingRetentionWatchdog` synchronously (`:1509`). The watchdog's interval stamp starts at zero, so retention is due immediately (`:1674-1678`). When the backup and store checks allow it, the pass reads every closed tracking bead from each store it visits, all before readiness. It caps successful deletions at 100 across stores. Nothing bounds the time spent listing or running the delete guard checks.

`start_ready_timeout` does not bound this. It only sets how long `gc start` / `gc register` wait, and when the startup watchdog dumps goroutines.

The comment on `startup-orders` says the step exists so due orders don't wait behind maintenance work. Retention is maintenance work that runs inside that step.

### Reproduction

`TestCityRuntimeRun_ReadyBeforeRetentionSweep` is one test-only commit on main 7a34e556e: https://github.com/A3Ackerman/gascity/commit/12f49ddf683815d10cdd83ae1d9cbd3ab34dc49f

The test does three things:
1. It blocks the retention read.
2. It requires `OnStarted` to fire anyway.
3. It pokes the runtime and requires the retention read to happen within 10 seconds after `OnStarted`.

```sh
go test ./cmd/gc -run '^TestCityRuntimeRun_ReadyBeforeRetentionSweep$' -count=10
```

On 7a34e556e it fails 10 times out of 10:

```
order-tracking retention read reached before the city reported ready; the startup pass was NOT deferred
```

### Environment

- Test: main at 7a34e556e, macOS arm64.
- Incident: Linux amd64, supervisor-managed city, Dolt sql-server beads store, default `delete_after_close` (7d).

### Proposed fix

Skip only the retention watchdog during `startup-orders`, and leave its interval stamp unchanged so retention is still due on the first steady-state tick. This is the same boot-maintenance deferral #3811 used for #3288. With that change, the test passed 20 times out of 20 locally.

An alternative is to take retention off the tick entirely, on its own goroutine with single-flight. That is more than this bug needs.

I'm happy to open a PR with the test.

Related:
- #2604: order dispatch starving the tick in steady state.
- #3926: order-tracking retention growth.

title: fix(beads): carry bd's blocked status through the read model
body:
## Problem

`mapBdStatus` collapses bd's six statuses to three, and the collapse erases `blocked`. Four read paths share the function (`BdStore` decode, `DoltliteReadStore`, `NativeDoltStore`, and `EncodeBeadEventPayload`), so no response can carry the state. One bead, three sources at one moment:

```
curl -s 'http://127.0.0.1:8372/v0/city/<name>/beads?limit=1000'
  -> {"id":"sc-lm3zj","status":"open"}
bd show sc-lm3zj --json   -> "status":"blocked"
bd list --limit 0 --json  -> "status":"blocked"
```

The whole-list histogram from that endpoint read 497 open, 3 in_progress, and 0 blocked, while bd reported 48 blocked in the same city. `in_progress` survives, so the projection is not collapsing everything; it loses `blocked` specifically. The dashboard then reported 99 beads as needing a human when 26 of them were finished work blocked only on a handoff claim.

The DTO's `is_blocked` column does not recover the state: it answers bd's different, dependency-derived question and reads 0 for explicitly blocked beads.

## Change

Widen the status set rather than compensate in the frontend. `mapBdStatus` returns `"blocked"`, so every reader sees it. `review` and `testing` still collapse to `open`, because no consumer distinguishes them.

`blocked` joins the open **set** instead of becoming a third terminal state, which keeps the change reporting-only:

- `beads.IsOpenStatus` reports membership in that set. The 38 demand, claim, dispatch, route-recovery, sling, and mail guards that mean "still open" ask it instead of comparing to `"open"`.
- `ListQuery.Matches` treats `Status:"open"` as the set. That is already what the native store's `ExcludeStatus{closed, in_progress}` filter returns, and `native_dolt_store_count.go` documents the mismatch. Exact equality there would have silently dropped every blocked bead from each `Status:"open"` list, changing demand, claim, and mail behavior.
- Ready stays narrower on purpose: `IsReadyCandidateForTier` still compares the status exactly, mirroring `nativeDoltOpenReadyStatuses`, because bd's own ready semantics exclude blocked (ga-3mv5d3).

The dashboard Beads page and the attention badge are untouched; both are correct on correct data.

## Consumer audit

51 non-test sites compared a status to `"open"`. 38 are guards on a decoded bead that must keep treating blocked as open, and they now call `IsOpenStatus`. The rest stay exact, each for a reason:

| Site | Why it stays exact |
| --- | --- |
| `beads.IsReadyCandidateForTier` | Mirrors `nativeDoltOpenReadyStatuses`; bd excludes blocked from ready. |
| `MemStore.Reopen`, `SQLiteStore.Reopen` | A blocked bead must still reopen to `open`. |
| `EncodeBeadEventPayload` | Restores an indefinite deferral, which only bd's `deferred` sets. |
| `session.sessionMatchesFilters` | Pinned twin-equivalence contract with `sessionMatchesFiltersInfo`; a non-closed session bead still matches through the `state` filter. |
| `native_dolt_store.go`, `native_dolt_store_count.go`, `caching_store_writes.go` | Query and write inputs, not decoded statuses. |

## Tests

- `internal/beads/blocked_status_test.go` pins blocked through the mapping, `normalizedBdReadState`, the open set, a `Status:"open"` list, an exact `Status:"blocked"` list, and the Ready exclusion.
- Repinned the two tables that asserted the old collapse: `TestBdStoreStatusMapping` and `TestNativeDoltStoreMapsUpstreamStatusesToGasCityContract`.
- `TestNativeDoltStoreListStatusOpenMatchesOpenNormalizedUpstreamStatuses` keeps its membership assertion; its per-row check now asserts open-set membership.
- `MemStore` was the one store that dropped a literal blocked row from an open list, so `TestCachingStorePartialPrimeRefusesUnknownDependencyStatus` changed premise. It now pins the refusal with a closed dependency, which genuinely is outside the primed snapshot, and a new `TestCachingStorePartialPrimeKnowsBlockedDependency` pins that a blocked dependency is inside it and still blocks its dependent.
- Refreshed the comments that described the old collapse, in product code and in the tests that model the hazard.

## Verification

```
gofmt -l ./cmd ./internal              # clean
go vet ./internal/beads ./cmd/gc ./internal/api
go test ./internal/beads/...           # ok
go test ./internal/api/...             # ok
go test ./internal/mail/... ./internal/dispatch/... ./internal/sling/... \
        ./internal/nudgequeue/... ./internal/session/... ./internal/orders/...   # ok
go test ./cmd/gc/                      # see below
```

`cmd/gc` reports 121 failures on this machine, and all of them are environmental: 118 fail because a local PATH guard refuses `git -c core.hooksPath` inside the worktree-reaper fixtures, two init tests fail on the same guard during `git clone`, and `TestStopManagedCityBoundsForcedShutdownWhenRuntimeHangs` misses a 120 ms timing budget. The three non-guard failures reproduce identically in an untouched checkout at base. The status-sensitive subset passes:

```
go test ./cmd/gc/ -run 'Blocked|Demand|RouteRecovery|DetachedOrphan|PoolIdle|NamedTrigger|Treadmill|AwakeBridge|SessionName'   # ok
```

`internal/runtime/herdr` does not compile at `ca8c28edc` (`panebinding_provider_test.go` return-value mismatches), which is unrelated to this change.

title: fix(opencode,mimocode): drain queued nudges once per turn
body:
## Summary

Fixes #5552. Supersedes the stale #5560 (same design, rebased onto current `main`, which had already moved the OpenCode hook to v6 for #5563) and extends it to the MiMo Code plugin, which has the identical shape.

OpenCode fires `experimental.chat.system.transform` from `Agent.generate`, once per model generation, and `chat.message` once more per user message. Both call `buildPrefix()`, so every tool call in a turn ran `gc nudge drain --inject` and `gc mail check --inject` again. Two consequences:

- The drain is consumptive, so the queue was emptied several times per turn and the drained items landed in whichever generation won the race.
- Each run re-opens the bead store (two unconditional opens in `resolveNudgeTarget` / `cmd_nudge.go:534`, one more in mail check, closed-inclusive session lists), so the cost scales with tool calls, not with prompts. On a seven-lane 1.4.1 city with the Dolt-backed store this measured ~18 new sql-server connections/s, ~165 queries/s, `dolt sql-server` at ~270% CPU and `gc doctor fork-rate` at 200–365 forks/s, with `show full processlist` nearly empty. Every other provider drains once per user prompt (`internal/hooks/config/README.md`); OpenCode and MiMo Code were the outliers.

The plugin now records the turn a user message opens (`message.updated` with `role === "user"`) and runs the two consumptive commands once per turn; later generations repeat only the cached prime, which is per-generation context and correct to repeat. With no known turn (events not delivered, payload without those fields) it drains every time as before, so nudges are never withheld. OpenCode hook → v7 with a `drainedTurnID` marker in `opencodeHookNeedsUpgrade`; MiMo Code hook → v3. CHANGELOG entry under Unreleased / Fixed.

The store-open cost itself (#5539, `bd_env.go:1652-1669`) is out of scope here; this PR removes the multiplier in front of it.

## Testing

- [x] `CGO_ENABLED=0 go test ./internal/hooks/ ./cmd/gc/ -run 'Embed|BuiltinPacks|Overlay|OpenCode'` pass; `golangci-lint run ./internal/hooks/...` 0 issues; `go vet` clean; `gofmt -l` empty. (`make check` as a whole did not run on this box: the Dolt/ICU CGO dependency needs `libicu-dev`, which I could not install without sudo. Happy to re-run if CI needs anything beyond the targeted packages.)
- [ ] `make check-docs` — no docs/navigation changes
- [ ] `make test-integration` — no runtime/controller changes; plugin-only behaviour, covered below
- [x] Harness that loads the plugin the way OpenCode does and fires 2 turns × (1 `chat.message` + 6 `system.transform`), with `GC_BIN` stubbed:

  | plugin | `nudge drain` calls | `mail check` calls | generations that re-injected drained nudges |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | main (v6) | 14 | 14 | 6/6 per turn |
  | this PR (v7) | 2 | 2 | 0/6 per turn (prime only) |

- [x] Same harness against a live 1.4.1 city store (`show global status like 'Connections' / 'Questions'` before/after, managed pool-lane identity):

  | plugin | new Dolt connections | queries |
  |---|---|---|
  | main (v6) | +4,988 | +35,842 |
  | this PR (v7) | +448 | +4,410 |

## Checklist

- [x] Linked an issue (#5552)
- [x] Added or updated tests for behavior changes (`hooks_test.go`: version bumps, `drainedTurnID` marker in the managed-install and needs-upgrade fixtures)
- [x] Updated docs for user-facing changes (CHANGELOG)
- [x] Breaking changes: none. Installed OpenCode plugins below v7 / without the marker are upgraded on the next reconcile with the usual numbered backup; session spawn already overwrites unconditionally.

title: fix(api): resolve a pool session's recorded runtime name in gc status (ga-7n2hhq)
body:
Fixes the false-outage class behind ga-7n2hhq: `gc status --json` reports
`running:false` for an agent whose seat is alive and working. On 2026-09-16
this reached the mayor as a false P0 against a `gascity/deployer` that was
working normally and had just passed the full suite.

## Root cause

`gc status` derived every agent's session name canonically
(`internal/api/handler_status.go:251` → `agent.SessionNameFor`). But a pool
instance's runtime name is minted by a **separate** derivation:
`poolRuntimeSessionName` (`cmd/gc/session_name_lookup.go:489`) steps aside
onto a `-pool` suffixed name when a configured named session reserves the
bare one, or for a transient slot.

That step-aside is *sanctioned* — it exists so a pool can coexist with a
configured named session on the same agent — and it is recorded on the
session bead. It cannot be re-derived from the agent identity. So status
probed `gascity--deployer` while the seat actually ran as
`gascity--deployer-pool`, `IsRunning` returned false, and a live seat was
reported dead.

Two independent derivations of one naming contract; only the create side
knew the whole rule.

## The session-snapshot timeout is NOT the cause

The incident report blamed the `partial:true` session-snapshot timeout. That
is coincident, not causal, and it is worth being explicit because the
obvious "fix" would not have prevented this:

1. **By source:** the `running` field comes from `statusProviderRunning` →
   `sp.IsRunning` (`handler_status.go:1091-1097`). It never reads the
   snapshot, so a snapshot timeout cannot change it.
2. **By experiment:** the tests here run with a **healthy** snapshot — they
   assert no `sessions:` partial error is present — and still reproduce
   `running:false`. The positive control (same capacity shape, same healthy
   snapshot, canonical session name) passes. The session *name* is the only
   variable that changes the verdict.

So reporting `running: null` under `partial:true` would not have prevented
this incident. It may have merit on its own, but it is a separate concern
and is deliberately not in this PR.

## Fix

New helper `statusRuntimeSessionName` resolves the runtime name from the
session snapshot the status path **already holds** — no new I/O. Strongest
evidence first:

1. a session bead sitting on the canonical name — today's behavior, kept
   exactly, so canonically named sessions are unaffected;
2. a bead whose recorded `agent_name` IS this instance — the shape
   production writes (`cmd/gc/build_desired_state.go:4836` sets
   `identityAgentName` to the qualified instance, falling back to the
   template);
3. for a single-instance identity, the one bead recorded against it.

Anything ambiguous falls back to the canonical name rather than guessing.

The data was already in hand: `statusSessionSnapshot` carries a `byTemplate`
index and `appendUnlimitedPoolSessionBeads` already used it — but returned
early for **any** bounded-capacity agent (`*maxSess >= 0`), which is exactly
the `min=0`/`max=1` shape that an explicit `MinActiveSessions` creates
(`internal/config/session_capacity.go:123`).

### Note for reviewers

`statusSessionQualifiedName` looks like the right matching helper and is
**not**: it maps `gascity--deployer-pool` to `gascity/deployer-pool`, not to
the agent identity `gascity/deployer`, so matching on it silently fails.
That is the trap a re-derivation of this fix would most likely fall into.

## Tests

`internal/api/handler_status_pool_identity_test.go` — 5 tests, each verified
**RED at a41b91a032** and **GREEN** with the change:

- `TestStatusReportsPoolSuffixedSessionAsRunning` — the incident
- `TestStatusReportsPoolSuffixedSessionAsRunningWithRecordedAgentName` — the
  bead shape production actually persists
- `TestStatusMapsEachPoolInstanceToItsOwnSession` — multi-instance; fails if
  instances are cross-wired onto each other's sessions
- `TestStatusReportsCanonicallyNamedSessionAsRunning` — positive control
- `TestStatusKeepsUnlimitedPoolAgentVisible` — positive control

Gates: full `internal/api` package passes (exit 0), `go vet` clean,
`go build ./...` clean, pre-commit hooks active and passed (`lint-changed`
0 issues), pre-push suite reported all fast jobs passed.

## Relationship to ga-rkbqnc.2.4 (open, ready-to-build)

Complementary, **not** duplicate. `ga-rkbqnc.2.4` normalizes
`SupportsInstanceExpansion` (create-side, `session_capacity.go`); its own
audit in `ga-rkbqnc.2.1` records that all five `internal/api` packages stay
green under that change. It does not touch this read-side resolution, and it
would not have fixed this — a live session keeps the name it was created
with. Different files, no collision.

## Scope / impact

No wire or API change (`StatusAgentDetail` is unchanged), no new
abstraction. Consumers using `gc status` as a liveness probe stop seeing
working pool seats as dead. Behavior for canonically named sessions is
unchanged by construction (resolution step 1).

title: bug: a requested named-session restart can leave a live, promptless runtime — start errors in start_call, never reaches post_start_observe, and nothing retries
body:
### Before you continue

- [x] I searched existing issues and did not find a duplicate.
- [x] I read the relevant docs and contributor guidance.

Searched: `resuming session: session already exists`, `post_start_observe`,
`restart-requested no such session`, `session reconciler race prompt`,
`session launched without prompt`, `unprimed session`,
`start_call provider_error session already exists`.

The two nearest hits are **not** this, and I want to be explicit about why,
because both look close:

- **#5593** (closed) matches on the error string `resuming session: session
  already exists`, but it is about `one_shot` **pool** sessions blocking their
  own runtime name after a normal exit. This is a **named** session being
  restarted on request.
- **#4382** (open) is also "born unprimed", but by a different mechanism:
  reconciler-spawned **formula step** sessions whose routing is stamped at
  `bead.created` so `nudge-on-route` never fires. Here the session is a named
  one, the restart was explicitly requested, and the start itself errors.

### Gas City version

`HEAD-e736d74d0` — source build of `e736d74d0` (2026-08-24), with a
source-built `bd` `1.1.0 (dev: main@bf97b73749ac)`.

### Environment

Linux, systemd `--user` supervisor, Dolt-backed stores, `claude` provider,
2 rigs (both suspended — a near-idle city). Named session `mayor`,
`lifecycle` restart-on-request via `gc handoff`.

### Reproduction

1. Have a named, controller-restartable session (here: `mayor`).
2. From inside it, request a restart — `gc handoff`, which sends mail to self
   and then `gc runtime request-restart`.
3. Observe the reconciler's stop/start pair in `supervisor.log`.

It does not reproduce on demand: this is a **race**, and it has now happened
twice in twelve days against ~119 healthy starts in the same log. I am filing
it because both occurrences leave the *same* distinctive signature, so the
signature is probably more useful to you than a recipe.

### Expected behavior

The restarted session receives its rendered template prompt as the first user
message, as it does on every healthy start.

### Actual behavior

The runtime starts and the prompt is never delivered. A `claude` process is
alive in the tmux session, attached and idle, with **zero user records in its
transcript**, and it stays that way indefinitely — 7m08s on this occurrence,
until a human ran `gc session reset mayor`. 15 minutes on the previous one.

Nothing retries: the session is up, so the reconciler is satisfied.

### Logs, screenshots, or traces

The failing restart, `~/.gc/supervisor.log`:

```
session reconciler: clearing restart-requested marker for mayor (bead bl-0odu):
    tmux -u: no such session: mayor
Stopped restart-requested session 'mayor'
session reconciler: provider-health registry unavailable for "claude-mayor";
    treating as green
session lifecycle: op=start wave=0 session=mayor template=mayor
    outcome=start_enqueued duration=0s
session reconciler: starting mayor: resuming session: session already exists:
    session "mayor"
session lifecycle: op=start wave=0 session=mayor template=mayor
    outcome=provider_error duration=351ms phases=[start_call=351ms]
    err=resuming session: session already exists: session "mayor"
Stopped restart-requested session 'mayor'
```

The successful manual reset seven minutes later, same session, same log:

```
session lifecycle: op=start wave=0 session=mayor template=mayor
    outcome=start_enqueued duration=0s
Woke session 'mayor'
session lifecycle: op=start wave=0 session=mayor template=mayor
    outcome=success duration=19.799s
    phases=[start_call=17.727s post_start_observe=2.072s]
```

**The discriminator is `post_start_observe`.** Every healthy start in this log
carries it (~5s + ~2.1s); the failed start has only `start_call` and no `Woke
session` line. The prompt appears to be delivered in that phase, so a start
that errors in `start_call` leaves a live, promptless runtime behind.

The 2026-09-04 occurrence has the same shape with a different error string —
`outcome=success duration=28ms phases=[start_call=28ms]`, no
`post_start_observe` — against ~5s + ~2.1s on the other 118 starts in that
window.

The event log tells the same story more compactly. A requested restart emits
`session.draining` then `session.woke`; across nine prior restarts of this
session the pair is always 32–68s apart, and on the failure the second event
never arrives:

```
14:55:08 -> 14:55:40  +32s      21:00:26 -> 21:01:02  +36s
15:14:44 -> 15:15:52  +68s      21:37:15 -> 21:37:49  +34s
16:39:43 -> 16:40:38  +55s      00:13:45 -> 00:14:44  +59s
18:38:57 -> 18:39:54  +57s      10:09:49 -> (none)
19:11:15 -> 19:11:52  +37s
```

### Additional context

**The apparent mechanism**, offered as a reading of the log rather than as a
claim about the code, which I have not read: the reconciler goes to clear the
restart marker and tmux reports the session already gone. Its bookkeeping then
treats the session as present on the following start — the start takes a
*resume* path — and the resume errors because by then a tmux session named
`mayor` exists again.

**Two things that might matter for the fix:**

1. `provider_error` here is not retried. Whatever the right recovery is, the
   current outcome is a permanently idle session that looks healthy to
   everything watching it.
2. `gc session reset` is a reliable recovery, and we have automated it locally
   behind a zero-user-records predicate. That is a workaround, not a fix, and
   it only works because a session with no user records has no state to lose.

**A detail that may help anyone else hitting this:** a queued nudge cannot
rescue such a session. Ours were dead-lettered with `queued nudge session
fence mismatch` about 29s in — the fence is the continuation epoch rather than
the session id, so a nudge queued across the restart boundary dies with the
old epoch. So the failure is not observable-and-recoverable through the nudge
path; the session has to be replaced.

title: bug: gc hook --claim work query can consume the whole claim window on a serialized shared dolt server while a direct bd claim completes in seconds
body:
## Title

```
bug: hook --claim work query can consume the whole claim window on a serialized shared dolt server while a direct bd claim completes in seconds
```

## Summary

On a multi-rig city backed by a single shared (serialized) Dolt sql-server, `gc hook --claim --json`
repeatedly exceeds ~110 s and appears hung to the agent, while the same claim performed directly
(`bd ready` + `bd update <id> --claim`) completes in ~2 s and a bare `gc hook <agent> --json` returns
in ~15 s. The claim window is sized from the work-query timeout plus the mutation timeout
(`hookClaimWindowDefault = hookWorkQueryTimeout + hookClaimMutationTimeout`, `cmd_hook_claim.go`),
and the work query is bounded at 150 s (`cmd_hook.go`, raised 60→150 s on 2026-08-14 because the
~6-leg sequential probe was already exceeding 30 s under load). The design therefore *schedules*
multi-minute claim latencies on exactly the deployments (one Dolt server serving every rig's store)
the docs recommend, and the agent-visible behavior is indistinguishable from a hang.

## Environment

- macOS 27.0 (arm64), gc 1.4.1 via Homebrew (`beads` pinned 1.2.2, in-process NativeDoltStore active)
- One managed Dolt sql-server (127.0.0.1) serving **10 rig databases + hq** for a 10-rig city
- `probe_concurrency` unset → default 8 concurrent bd subprocess probes
  (`internal/config/config.go`: "bd serializes on a shared dolt sql-server, so unbounded
  parallelism causes contention" — the config comment itself names this contention mode)
- Contention source: pool scale-check + work-query probes from concurrent worker sessions and the
  reconciler, all hitting the same serialized server

## Reproduction

1. Run a multi-rig city (≥4 rigs, ~10 databases) on one shared Dolt server; have several workers
   and the reconciler issuing probes concurrently.
2. From a worker session run `gc hook <agent> --claim --json`.
3. Under load the command runs >110 s (observed repeatedly in production use, 2026-09-15); with the
   city idle the same command returns in ~11 s, and the non-claim hook returns in ~7-15 s.
4. Independently: `bd ready --json` (~1.4 s) and `bd update <id> --claim` (~2 s) complete against
   the same contended server.

Smallest observable differential (same server, same minute, idle city):

| Command | Wall time |
|---|---|
| `gc hook <agent> --json` (no claim) | ~7 s |
| `gc hook <agent> --claim --json` | ~11 s (loaded: >110 s) |
| `bd ready --json` | ~1.4 s |
| `bd update <id> --claim` | ~2 s |

## Expected behavior

An atomic claim should not be starved by the discovery probe. The claim CAS is a cheap single-store
mutation (`hookClaimMutationTimeout = 10 s`, correctly bounded); the expensive part is the
*federated routed-work query* in front of it, which re-runs the multi-leg probe (config comment:
"~6 sequential bd/store round-trips") on every claim attempt, serially competing with the very
contention it generates. Expected: claim latency stays O(mutation), discovery cost is capped or
cached, and a claim that finds work quickly claims it quickly.

## Actual behavior

- The work query legitimately runs up to 150 s (`hookWorkQueryTimeout`), and the claim window is
  derived from it (160 s total), so >110 s claim attempts are *by design* rather than a failure
  signal — but from the agent's seat they are indistinguishable from a hung process, and the
  documented work loop ("run `gc hook --claim`, repeat after closing") serializes this cost into
  every work item.
- Under concurrent probe load the serialized Dolt server makes each probe leg slower, so the
  system is at its worst exactly when the most workers are trying to claim: probe concurrency 8
  amplifies load; the raised 150 s bound converts the amplification into multi-minute waits.
- gascity's own history anticipates this shape: `cmd_hook.go` records 850+ `session.work_query_failed`
  events at the old 60 s bound ("every hook starved while `gc ready` run standalone returned the
  routed rows"). The bound was raised rather than the round-trip count reduced ("the real cure
  remains ga-4qdfn (fewer round-trips, faster reader)").

## Evidence

- Timing table above (production Mac, gc 1.4.1; >110 s observations from loaded city 2026-09-15)
- `cmd_hook.go:907-926` — `hookWorkQueryTimeout = 150s` with the 850+-events starvation history in
  the comment
- `cmd_hook_claim.go:58-85` — `hookClaimMutationTimeout = 10s`,
  `hookClaimWindowDefault = hookWorkQueryTimeout + hookClaimMutationTimeout`, comment: "a loaded
  multi-rig city's federated probe legitimately runs tens of seconds"
- `internal/config/config.go:2602-2607` — `probe_concurrency` default 8, comment naming bd
  serialization on a shared dolt sql-server as the contention cause
- `internal/doltpool/pool.go` — pooled *sql.DB handles with ReadTimeout/WriteTimeout 30 s exist for
  gc's Go-native paths; note `internal/api/convoy_sql.go:buildDoltDSN` sets dial `Timeout` but no
  `ReadTimeout`/`WriteTimeout`, so that path can hold a dead connection until TCP gives up
  (related, possibly distinct issue — flagging for triage)
- Transient CLOSE_WAIT connections on the client side observed during loaded windows (consistent
  with a response the client never reads back; not present at idle) — `lsof -nP -iTCP:<dolt-port>`

## Additional context

- Workers on this city now bypass `gc hook --claim` entirely (`bd ready` + `bd update --claim`)
  because the direct path is ~50× faster; this routes around atomic-claim bookkeeping, which is
  the integration smell that made us file.
- Possibly related known issue (same command, different failure mode): idle workers re-claim beads
  parked blocked-on-human, churning park/reclaim loops. Both suggest the claim protocol's
  discovery stage needs the rework ga-4qdfn anticipated.
- Suggested directions (maintainer's call): split claim into discover-fast (bounded, cheap,
  cache-friendly) + claim-fast (CAS, already bounded); let `--claim` accept a hint bead id;
  reduce probe round-trips per the existing ga-4qdfn note; expose claim-window progress so a
  multi-minute wait is distinguishable from a hang.

## Mitigation we ship locally (for the runbook PR, not upstream)

Documented in the cityworker work loop (`city/agents/cityworker/prompt.template.md`, "Work Loop →
KNOWN ISSUE 2026-09-15"): if `gc hook --claim` exceeds 60 s, fall back to
`gc bd ready --unassigned --sort oldest -t task --json` + `gc bd update <id> --claim`, verifying
assignee afterwards (command shape verified against gc 1.4.1: `--sort oldest` is the valid value,
not `created_at`). Race window acknowledged and accepted at city scale; explicit drain/no_work
results are still honored, timeouts are never treated as empty queues, and `gc hook --claim`
remains the primary path.

title: bug: pool seats retired mid-claim because alias-form claims are invisible to the keep-awake and drain-ack close gates
body:
### Gas City version
main `ed146d8d9` (2026-09-02); the unit-level reproduction also holds on `af596339d` (2026-09-14).

### Environment
Linux (Fedora 44), tmux runtime, opencode-backed pool agents (gastown pack `gastown.polecat`, `max_active_sessions = 10`).

### Reproduction
1. Route several beads to a pool template; seats claim them with `gc hook --claim`. The claim's `assignee` is the seat alias (`GC_ALIAS`, e.g. `rig/gastown.nux`), while the session bead's `session_name` is the tmux form (`rig--gastown__nux`).
2. Let template demand drop (other beads finish) while one seat still holds an `in_progress` claim.
3. Watch the reconciler: that seat is closed with `session drained: pool slot retired by reconciler`, followed immediately by `bead.dead_assignee_reopened` for its claim, and a fresh seat re-primes from zero.

### Expected behavior
A seat holding an `in_progress` claim stays desired (`assigned-work`), is counted by `countAssignedScaleSlots`, and the drain-ack close gate sees its claim.

### Actual behavior
`sessionAssignmentIdentifierRaw`/`RawInfo` and `ComputeAwakeSet`'s `sessionAssigneeMatches` only compare `{bead id, session_name, configured named identity}`. Claims are written under the alias (`session.AssigneeIdentifier` is alias-first), so every pool seat reads as work-free and becomes a scale-down victim. The orphan-release path (`session.AssigneeIdentities`) already honours the alias, which is why the reopen follows the drain within seconds.

### Logs, screenshots, or traces
One city, 24 h, tributary pool: 122 polecat stops, 89 `bead.dead_assignee_reopened`, mean seat life ~20 min, 15–25 % of seats under 3 min; identical under three model providers, so not model-related. With the alias honoured in those three sites (see the linked PR): 22 stops and 0 reopens over the next 24 h.

### Additional context
`TestAssignmentGuardsIgnoreTransientPoolSlotAliases` states slot-form aliases (`<pool>-<n>`) must never keep a session alive. The PR keeps that guard and honours namepool aliases only. If the preferred fix is to claim under a stable identity instead (bead id / session_name), I'm happy to rework it that way.

title: fix(formulas): append work-bead notes instead of replacing them
body:
## Problem

Five core-pack formula steps pass `--notes` to `$WORK_BEAD_ID`. `bd update --notes` replaces the notes field, so each of these steps discards any notes the bead already carries. On 2026-09-15 one such write destroyed four coordinator notes on a live issue; the operator recovered them from `dolt_history_issues`, which worked only because someone noticed in time.

beads PR https://github.com/gastownhall/beads/pull/6583 makes `bd update --notes` refuse the write when the target bead already holds different, non-empty notes. Once that lands, these five steps fail instead of clobbering. This change moves them to `--append-notes`, which preserves the history and already works with the current `bd`.

## Change

`--notes` becomes `--append-notes` at the five sites that target `$WORK_BEAD_ID`:

- `internal/bootstrap/packs/core/formulas/mol-do-work.toml` (the shipped close and the no-op close)
- `internal/bootstrap/packs/core/formulas/mol-polecat-commit.toml`
- `internal/bootstrap/packs/core/formulas/mol-polecat-report.toml`
- `internal/bootstrap/packs/core/formulas/mol-prompt-synth.toml`

`mol-do-work.toml` keeps `--notes` for `$GC_BEAD_ID` and `$DRAIN_BEAD_ID`, because a step wisp and a drain bead hold no prior notes.

`TestCoreMolPolecatReportWriteReportStepRecordsNoteAndAvoidsPRFlow` pinned the literal substring `--notes`, which `--append-notes` does not contain, so the expected substring moves with the flag. The assertion's intent is unchanged: the step records the report on the work bead.

`internal/bdflags/bdflags.go` already lists `--append-notes` as a value flag for `bd update`, so `gc bd` forwards it today with no other change.

## Verification

title: fix(pool): treat a live session's currently_processing_bead_id as first-party proof of ownership
body:
## Summary
- Fixes #6362 (P1): a replacement session stayed awake and continuously reported `currently_processing_bead_id=<bead>`, while the work bead's own `Assignee` still named the drained predecessor session. The dead-assignee reopen sweep fired against a bead a live session was actively executing.
- Traced the actual mechanism rather than trusting the reporter's framing of `gc.session_id` as the operative field -- it isn't. `gc.session_id` is a diagnostic metadata field (`stampHookClaimIdentity`), written once at claim time for dashboard display, not the liveness signal. The real mechanism is `releaseOrphanedPoolAssignments` (`pool_session_name.go`), which checks the work bead's `Assignee` against every identity a currently-open session answers to (ID, session_name, configured named identity, alias, alias history). None of those forms is retroactively updated when a *new* session bead succeeds a different, now-closed session bead under the same logical role without an intervening `gc hook --claim` -- the existing alias/alias-history continuity mechanism only preserves identity across a rename *within one bead's own lifetime*, never across a bead replacement.
- Checked whether a separate wake-decision matcher (`sessionAssigneeMatches` in `compute_awake_set.go`) already recognizes this case before designing a new mechanism -- it does, for any session whose identity is the assignee. The replacement's own `currently_processing_bead_id`, stamped by `recordCurrentBeadIDOnWake` only once some pass has already resolved this exact bead as its anchor, is therefore concrete, current, first-party evidence of live ownership independent of the `Assignee` string.

## Fix
- `releaseOrphanedPoolAssignments` now builds an index of every open session's `currently_processing_bead_id` and skips release for any work bead in that set, before the existing identity-matching gates run. Purely additive -- never causes an *extra* release, only prevents one the existing checks would otherwise fire. Same "retain rather than reap" principle the function already applies via its `protectedWakeWork` guard, reused rather than reinvented.

## Test plan
- `TestReleaseOrphanedPoolAssignments_SkipsWhenReplacementSessionReportsCurrentlyProcessing` -- the direct regression, mirroring the reporter's exact repro shape.
- `TestReleaseOrphanedPoolAssignments_ReleasesWhenOpenSessionReportsDifferentCurrentBead` -- proves the new check doesn't over-protect: a live session processing a *different* bead must not shield an unrelated stale assignment.
- Full existing `TestReleaseOrphanedPoolAssignments_*` suite (40+ tests): green, including every alias/named-identity/store-scoping edge case.
- Full `cmd/gc` package: one pre-existing failure (`TestRunStartDriftCheck_DelegatedTryRestartTimeoutThenReplacementSucceeds`, systemd-only environmental flake, confirmed unrelated against unmodified `origin/main`). `go build ./...` and `go vet ./cmd/gc/...` clean.

title: fix(nudge): route wait-idle and backstop nudges through the pending-interaction refusal
body:
Closes the "refuse" half of #2892 — the acceptance criterion in the issue body (Option A / T-004), scoped to the refusal itself.

## The problem

A session sitting at an approval or selection prompt is waiting on a human, not stalled. Delivering a nudge there types into the open prompt and answers on the operator's behalf.

The refusal already exists. `sendLocked` (`internal/session/chat.go`) and `Submit` (`internal/session/submit.go`) both consult `pendingInteractionLocked` before delivering. Three paths reach the same provider without it:

- `tryWaitIdleNudgeLocked`
- `tryWaitIdleNudgeLiveOnlyLocked`
- the shared backstop delivery in `cmd/gc/nudge_backstop.go`, which serves the claim, continuation and execution lanes

This routes those three through the existing check. It adds no second opinion about what "busy" means, and no new detection heuristic.

## Given / When / Then

- **Given** a session at an approval prompt, **when** a wait-idle nudge is attempted, **then** it returns `ErrPendingInteraction` and no nudge is delivered.
- **Given** a backstop lane with a seat at a prompt, **when** the lane would nudge, **then** it skips, logs why, and does not consume an attempt.
- **Given** a dormant session with no prompt, **when** a wait-idle nudge is attempted, **then** the managed wake still proceeds and the nudge lands.
- **Given** a pane probe that fails, **when** the backstop would nudge, **then** it skips and says so rather than assuming the seat is idle.

## Two ordering decisions worth review

**In the session paths the guard sits after `ensureRunning`**, as `sendLocked`'s does. A dormant session has no pane to probe, so checking first turns a managed wake into an error. `TestTryWaitIdleNudgeStillWakesDormantSession` pins the *call order* rather than the outcome — a fake reports no pending interaction for a session that does not exist, while a real pane probe returns `ErrSessionNotFound`, so an outcome-only assertion passes even with the guard misplaced.

**In the backstop the guard sits before the attempt reservation.** `reserve` writes ahead of delivery, so refusing after it would burn one of the bounded attempts on a nudge that was never sent.

## Failure direction

The backstop refuses on probe error as well as on a confirmed prompt, and prints which. The directions are not symmetric: skipping costs one tick, because the backstop re-evaluates the same seat on its next pass, while delivering into an open prompt cannot be taken back. Both refusals are visible on stdout rather than silent.

## Scope

`internal/session/chat.go` (+12), `cmd/gc/nudge_backstop.go` (+34), plus tests. No config surface, no new provider capability.

## Related work

- #2892 — the issue; this implements the refusal half of Option A / T-004. The detection-widening half (treating an open selection menu as not-idle at the CLI gate) is deliberately **not** here: it needs a single predicate shared with `internal/runtime/dialog.go` and live validation, and it would obscure this change.
- #6302 — extracted the backstop delivery loop into `runNudgeBackstop`, which is why one guard now covers all three lanes.
- #6347 / #6355 — nudge delivery observability and the no-retry-on-delivered contract; this refuses before delivery, so neither is affected.
- #3426 / #3427 — dismissing known dialogs. Complementary and orthogonal: those remove a dialog that can be dismissed, this refuses to type into one that cannot.

title: perf(beads): stop re-Getting deferred beads on every live list (ga-bhm5uq)
body:
## Summary

`staleLiveCacheIDs` marked **every indefinitely-deferred cached bead** stale on
**every** status-filtered live list, and the `backing.Get` that followed could
never clear it. This is a fixed point, not staleness — the refresh cannot
converge, by construction.

## The asymmetry

| leg | where the status filter is applied | result for a deferred bead |
|---|---|---|
| **List** | inside `bd`, in bd's own vocabulary, **before** normalization | `bd list --status=open` never returns it |
| **Get** | normalized **after** the read | `bd show` returns `deferred` → `Status: "open"` |

`mapBdStatus` (`internal/beads/bdstore.go:1197`) collapses every bd status that
is not `closed`/`in_progress` onto Gas City's `"open"`, with the deferral kept
out-of-band in `Bead.IndefinitelyDeferred` (`normalizedBdReadState`, `:1211`).
`ListQuery.Matches` (`internal/beads/query.go:254-260`) filters on `b.Status`
alone and never consults that flag.

So, per live list, per deferred bead:

1. absent from the fresh list → not in `freshIDs`
2. cached `Status` is `"open"` → `query.Matches(bead)` is true
3. → marked stale → one `bd show` subprocess
4. the fresh copy normalizes back to `Status: "open"`
5. `absorbFreshLocked` writes it unconditionally (`caching_store.go:489`)
6. → step 2, forever

Absorbing cannot break the loop, because the fresh copy is identical to the
cached one in the only field the query filters on.

## Evidence

**Unit (new test, fails before / passes after):**

```
live-list refresh never converges: 3 further identical live lists issued
3 more bd show calls for ga-deferred1 (cached Status="open"
IndefinitelyDeferred=true).
```

**Live controller** (pid 2465414, three `/proc` sampling windows):

- In a single 7-minute window, **763 distinct bead ids re-Got, 753 of them
  (98.7%) `deferred`** — that is **93.8% of the store's entire 803-bead deferred
  population**, re-Got inside one window. Store holds 4311 open / **803
  deferred** / 23 in_progress / 7 blocked.
- **144 of one window's 154 ids (93.5%) recurred 25 minutes later**, across many
  ticks — the set does not churn.
- **282 of 285** sampled deferred beads were last modified **28 days earlier**,
  so no new deferral events explain the traffic.

The release sweep issues one such live list **per work assignment**, which is
what made it run 262-411 s and release nothing (ga-s3cnmy).

## The fix

Skip a cached row whose own recorded deferral already explains its absence from
a status-filtered backing list. Getting it cannot change either fact.

The guard is `query.Status != ""` deliberately: an **unfiltered** live list
(`Status: ""`) genuinely does return deferred rows from bd, so absence there is
real news (deleted/closed) and must still trigger a Get.

**Nothing is lost.** A deferral that later closes is still reconciled by
`recoverMissingFromList`, which scans with an **empty** `Status`
(`cacheFullScanQuery`, `caching_store_reconcile.go:61`) where bd does return
deferred rows. The first live list after a deferral still costs one Get — that
is the cache learning the new state — and it now converges.

## Related

Builds on #5905, which introduced `IndefinitelyDeferred` for this exact
normalization hazard on the ready-queue path. `staleLiveCacheIDs` was the site
it did not reach.

## Not fixed here

bd's `blocked` status collapses to `"open"` the same way but normalization
leaves **no marker** behind, so it cannot be fixed by the same predicate. 7
beads against 803 deferred in this store — 99.1% of the waste is deferral.
Tracked separately.

## Testing

- [x] `go test ./internal/beads/... -count=1` — all `ok`
- [x] `go vet ./internal/beads/... ./cmd/gc/...` — clean
- [x] `.githooks/pre-commit` ran on the staged change (`lint-changed`: 0 issues,
      codegen, `go vet ./...`)

title: perf(gc): decline the revision snapshot in the hosted-credential probe (ga-s3cnmy)
body:
## What

`citySelectsHostedBeadsCredentialProvider` (`cmd/gc/bd_env.go`) loads `city.toml`
to read one boolean off the storage binding and discards the Provenance on the
same line. It never computes a `config.Revision()`, so it can never observe the
load-time revision snapshot — but the default load builds one anyway, and
building it reads and SHA-256s **every file of every pack directory,
recursively** (`captureRevisionSnapshot` → `packContentHashRecursive`, which
`internal/config/revision.go` calls with `useCache=false`).

That probe runs on the env/runner construction path for **every `bd`
subprocess** — and twice per invocation, from both `applyHostedBeadsCredentialEnv`
(`:614`) and `beadsCommandRunnerForHostedCity` (`:660`).

This passes `config.LoadOptions{SkipRevisionSnapshot: true}` there, and adds a
source-level guard test.

## Why — measured, not inferred (ga-s3cnmy)

Investigating a reconcile tick of 5.5–8 min on the `gc-management` controller
(deployed `gc ca73feb679`, pid 2465414, 2026-09-16).

**The controller is CPU-bound on its own work, not waiting on `bd`.**
`/proc/<pid>/stat` over one 45 s window — fields 14/15 are the process's own
utime/stime, 16/17 its reaped children's:

| | cpu-seconds in 45 s |
|---|---|
| controller's own | **129.75** (288% of a core) |
| every child process combined (`bd`, `ps`, …) | **24.17** (50% of a core) |

`perf record -F 199 --call-graph=fp`, two independent captures in **different**
tick phases (60 s/18200 samples; 45 s/31781 samples), inclusive:

| symbol | capture 1 | capture 2 |
|---|---|---|
| `config.LoadWithIncludesOptions` | 72.89% | 72.74% |
| `citySelectsHostedBeadsCredentialProvider` | 58.76% | 58.19% |
| `captureRevisionSnapshot` / `packContentHashRecursive` | 29.16% / 29.02% | |
| `sha256.blockSHANI` (self) | 15.92% | 15.40% |
| BurntSushi/toml lexer+parser (self, summed) | ~13.2% | ~12.4% |

Caller histogram for `LoadWithIncludesOptions`:
`citySelectsHostedBeadsCredentialProvider` 12998 samples (80.4%),
`loadPrematerializedCityConfig` 3170 (19.6%).

Per-load cost against this city's real `city.toml` (n=8, warmed):

| | per call |
|---|---|
| default (as called before) | **94.55 ms** |
| `SkipRevisionSnapshot: true` | **38.77 ms** (−59%) |

## Precedent

#4917 added `SkipRevisionSnapshot` for exactly this caller shape and scoped its
guard test to `cmd_agent.go`, saying in the test's own comment that the other
Provenance-discarding call sites were out of scope "for later". This is one of
those, and it is the hottest one in the controller.

## Safety

`LoadWithIncludes` is literally `LoadWithIncludesOptions(fs, path, LoadOptions{})`,
and `SkipRevisionSnapshot` is read in exactly one place (`compose.go:863`), gating
only `prov.captureRevisionSnapshot(...)`. The returned `*City` is unchanged, and
this caller discards the Provenance. No value can differ.

## Why a source-level guard test

Same reason `TestCityConfigLoadersDeclineTheRevisionSnapshot` is source-level:
reverting to the default returns an identical config and passes every functional
test. Nothing fails — it only gets slower, which is precisely the regression a
suite does not otherwise catch. Verified RED before the change, GREEN after.

## Scope — what this does NOT fix

Three larger findings from the same investigation are recorded on `ga-s3cnmy`
and each needs its own bead:

1. The remaining ~39 ms/load is `expandPacks` + TOML parse, still paid per `bd`
   subprocess. The real fix is memoizing the boolean itself across its 6
   non-test call sites, which needs an invalidation story for runtime config
   reload — an architecture call.
2. `liveWorkAssignmentAssigneeMatches` (`cmd/gc/work_assignment.go:334`) issues a
   full `List(Status, Live, TierBoth)` and linear-scans it to check **one** bead's
   assignee. It sits in a release path that clears assignees, so it is not a
   mechanical edit.
3. `CachingStore.refreshCachedBeads` re-`Get`s every cached-but-absent bead on
   every `Live` list and never converges — measured 3,227 `bd show` calls over
   893 distinct ids in 11 minutes, most re-fetched 3–6×.

This is also **not** a `release_orphaned_pool_assignments`-specific bug: capture 2
landed in a different phase (`runDetachedOrphanBackstop`) and shows the same
pathology at the same percentages. Every phase issuing a `Live` list pays it.

## Caveat

The improvement is measured at the config-load layer and by perf attribution, not
as a before/after tick time on a rebuilt controller — that needs a `gc` deploy,
and the deploy point is currently frozen behind the reaper type-scope guard
(`9296d22db8` is an ancestor of `origin/main` but not of the deployed
`ca73feb679`). Re-run `supbd-sampler.sh` at its own 200 ms cadence plus one perf
capture after the next deploy to confirm the magnitude.

title: fix(dolt): retry the health SQL probe and report client errors, not zeros
body:
## The problem

`gc dolt health --json` decides `server.reachable` from **one** bounded `dolt sql -q "SELECT 1"` call, with the client's stderr sent to `/dev/null`, and reports a per-database count as `0` whenever its client call fails. A single transient client failure on a healthy server therefore reads as `reachable: false` with `databases: []` (the database scan is skipped), or as `commits: 0`, and nothing records why.

That matters because consumers treat those values as measurements:

- `gc dolt health-check` (the `dolt-health` order) exits non-zero on `reachable == false`, recording an order failure.
- Patrol automation escalates `reachable == false` as CRITICAL, and the usual next runbook step is a Dolt restart. One bad sample can page for — and invite a restart of — a server that is fine.

### Observed

On a managed server that stayed up throughout (same PID before, during and after):

- One sample returned rc=0 with `running: true`, `reachable: false`, `latency_ms: 0`, `databases: []`.
- The next 39 samples over four minutes were all healthy: 9 full `gc dolt health --json` runs plus 30 direct `SELECT 1` probes, 41–105 ms each, at load average 10.8. Alternating cwd made no difference, and the Dolt log had nothing but baseline `io.ReadFull` timeouts for the window.
- The same generator produced an earlier single sample reporting `commits: 0` for a database whose `dolt_log` held 802 rows; five samples right after read it correctly.

The cause of the failed call is still unknown, and that is the point: stderr was discarded, so nothing recorded it.

## The change

- **Retry the reachability probe.** `SELECT 1` is retried up to `GC_DOLT_HEALTH_PROBE_ATTEMPTS` times (default 3), `GC_DOLT_HEALTH_PROBE_RETRY_SECS` apart (default 1), each attempt still bounded at 5s. `latency_ms` stays the round trip of the attempt that answered, so a retry cannot inflate it past the overload threshold.
- **Keep the client's error.** New `server.probe_attempts` and `server.probe_error` (the last failed attempt's stderr, normalized to one printable-ASCII line, capped at 300 bytes, JSON-escaped). `run_bounded`'s timeout is named when it fired (124, or 137 when `--kill-after` escalated). The error is kept even when a retry recovers, so a transient is visible without reading as an outage.
- **A missed count is unknown, not zero.** A count probe that fails, times out, or returns no number reports `null` plus `databases[].probe_error`. `result.schema.json` allows `null` for both counts.
- **Human output** says `running (PID …, port …) but not answering SQL after N attempt(s): <error>` instead of printing a latency for a server that never answered, and prints `unknown` for a null count.
- **`gc dolt health-check`** appends `attempts=` and `error=` to its failure message, so the order's recorded failure says why.

Cost: against a wedged server the worst case rises from one 5s bound to three. `TestHealthScriptIsBounded` goes from about 5s to 17.1s, inside its existing 45s budget.

## Tests

New `examples/bd/dolt/health_probe_test.go`, using a fake `dolt` on PATH whose failures carry JSON-hostile bytes (quotes, a backslash, a newline, a tab):

- **positive arm** — exactly one failed `SELECT 1`, then success: the report stays `reachable: true` with `probe_attempts: 2`, the failed attempt's error retained, and the database scan still runs.
- **negative arm** — a client that always fails: `reachable: false` after 3 attempts, with the client's error in both the JSON and the human output, and `databases: []`. Also covers `GC_DOLT_HEALTH_PROBE_ATTEMPTS=1` and a timeout whose client prints nothing.
- **counts** — a failed or non-numeric commits probe reports `null` (never 0) with the reason in `databases[].probe_error`, while the sibling count still reports its own value.
- **schema** — every outcome validates against `commands/health/schemas/result.schema.json`.

Both arms are required: testing only the healthy path would pass against the unfixed script.

Mutation-checked — each of these fails at least one of the new tests: dropping the retry (the positive arm then reads `reachable: false`), discarding the ping's stderr, defaulting a failed count back to 0, dropping `health-check`'s error, and reverting the schema to integer-only counts. The unmutated control passes 17/17.

### What I ran

- `go test ./examples/bd/dolt/` — 317/317 pass, including `TestHealthScriptIsBounded`, `TestHealthScriptJSONAlwaysExitsZero` and the portable-timestamp tests.
- `go test ./cmd/gc/ -run TestBuiltinDatabaseEnumeratorsSkipManagedProbeDatabase` — pass.
- `go vet ./examples/bd/dolt/` clean; `make lint-changed` (golangci-lint 2.12.0) 0 issues, verified live by injecting an errcheck violation; `golangci-lint fmt` clean.
- Live, with the real `dolt` client: against a healthy managed server the report reads reachable with `probe_attempts: 1` and real counts; against a closed port it reads unreachable after 3 attempts with the client's real "connection refused" text captured.

**Not run:** the whole-repo `make test-fast-parallel` fan-out that `.githooks/pre-push` fires. This host runs a live city, and the change touches no production Go code — only two shell commands, a schema, and a new test file — so I ran the package that owns them plus the one `cmd/gc` test that reads the script. CI's full suite still covers what I skipped.

## Known residual (not in this PR)

For a configured **external** endpoint, `external_database_names()` still sends `SHOW DATABASES` stderr to `/dev/null`, so a failed catalog query reads as `databases: []`. That is the same class as the counts fixed here; it needs the enumeration moved out of the pipeline subshell to carry an error, and I left it out to keep this change reviewable. Happy to follow up if you'd like it in the same PR.

title: bug: persistent named sessions skip the routed pool-demand probe entirely (GC_SESSION_ORIGIN gate) — routed work invisible to the session that owns it (v1.4.1; fix believed shipped in #6255, unreleased)
body:
# Upstream report — persistent named sessions skip the routed pool-demand probe entirely (`GC_SESSION_ORIGIN` gate) — routed work invisible to the session that owns it (v1.4.1; fix believed shipped in #6255)

**Filed:** 2026-09-16 by BeauBoorman on behalf of our fleet's city workers. Internal bead: ci-uioz (with owner ruling authorizing upstream filing after adversarial review — review verdict: APPROVE, 2026-09-16). Sibling report: hold-label claim churn (filed same day, same fix commit).

## Title

```
bug: persistent named sessions exit the hook before the routed pool-demand probe — work routed to the session itself is never discovered (v1.4.1; fix believed shipped in #6255, unreleased)
```

## Summary

On gc 1.4.1 (Homebrew), the generated `gc hook` prompt gates the routed pool-demand probe
behind `GC_SESSION_ORIGIN`: any session whose origin is neither `ephemeral` nor empty
short-circuits with `exit 0` before the probe runs. Persistent named sessions — the mayor
seat in our city, for example — therefore never see unassigned beads routed to them via
`gc.routed_to` in their hook, so escalated work stalls until someone discovers it manually.
We hit this in production: dog-escalated order work routed to `gastown__mayor` sat undiscovered
across two doctor-degraded episodes (2026-09-04/05) before manual discovery.

The correct underlying query is not in question — `bd ready --metadata-field
gc.routed_to=gastown__mayor --unassigned` returns the beads; it is purely the origin gate in
the generated hook that hides them from exactly the session whose name they carry.

This is not a local config error: the gate is embedded in the shipped binary, and upstream
tests introduced with ac8f6c6c (PR #6255) describe the same defect as their own discovery
(ga-6wkhl, the "olivia" specimen) and fix it. We are filing to (1) contribute production
validation from a bottle install, and (2) ask that the fix reach a release — no tag contains
it and the brew stable formula still ships 1.4.1.

## Environment

- macOS 27.0 (arm64); gc 1.4.1 via Homebrew (`/opt/homebrew/Cellar/gascity/1.4.1`)
- 10-rig city, one managed Dolt sql-server serving 10 rig databases + hq
- Affected seat: persistent named session `gastown__mayor` (`GC_SESSION_ORIGIN=named`,
  `GC_ALIAS=gastown__mayor`)
- Episodes: 2026-09-04 and 2026-09-05 (order work routed to the mayor seat discovered only
  manually); binary validation 2026-09-13

## Reproduction

1. Run a city with a persistent named session (e.g. the mayor seat) and a bead that is
   unassigned with `gc.routed_to` = that session's name.
2. As the named session, run `gc hook <agent> --json`.
3. The hook output contains no reference to the routed bead: the hook prompt's steps 1-3
   (assigned / existing-assignment probes) match nothing (the bead is unassigned), and the
   routed pool-demand probe never runs because of the origin gate.
4. Confirm the data plane disagrees: `bd ready --metadata-field gc.routed_to=<name>
   --unassigned --json` returns the bead.

### Root-cause evidence (binary, v1.4.1)

`strings /opt/homebrew/Cellar/gascity/1.4.1/bin/gc` contains the generated gate verbatim:

```
case "$GC_SESSION_ORIGIN" in ephemeral|"") ;; *) exit 0 ;; esac
```

i.e. every non-ephemeral origin exits the hook before any pool-demand probe. The 1.4.1
binary contains zero occurrences of `namedSelfTargetAdmit`, `PoolDemandServeRules`, or
`heldLabelCountJQ`.

## Root cause (upstream source, post-fix view)

`internal/config/workquery.go` (edge @ 06d073fe) emits the gate via
`poolDemandOriginGateScript()`. On edge it reads:

```sh
case "$GC_SESSION_ORIGIN" in ephemeral|"") ;; *) [ -n "$GC_ALIAS" ] && [ "$1" = "$GC_ALIAS" ] || exit 0 ;; esac
```

The added `namedSelfTargetAdmit` arm (`[ -n "$GC_ALIAS" ] && [ "$1" = "$GC_ALIAS" ]`)
admits a non-ephemeral session to the routed tier only when the probe target equals its own
claim alias — with an empty alias failing closed, and named+pool hybrids staying gated
(their `PoolName != GC_ALIAS`). The design comment documents the identity alignment:
`poolDemandTarget()` ($1), `RoutedToIdentity()` (the claim-match primary), and `GC_ALIAS`
all resolve to the same `QualifiedName()` for a plain named session, so the admitted work
is exactly the work the session's own claim path accepts, routed to itself, and nothing
routed elsewhere.

Regression coverage: `internal/config/workquery_named_routed_gate_test.go` pins the C2
defect (ga-6wkhl) with a fake bd whose only ready work is a single `gc.routed_to`-routed
frontier bead — if the origin gate still short-circuits, the bead can never surface.

## Upstream status (why we believe this is already fixed on main)

Commit ac8f6c6c (PR #6255, merged 2026-09-12) carries the gate widening above.

**Release gap:** `git tag --contains ac8f6c6c` is empty; latest release is v1.4.1
(2026-08-15, predates the fix); Homebrew `gascity` stable = 1.4.1 (bottled). The rolling
`edge` tag is a moving main pointer, not a consumption release for bottle installs.

## Impact

- Order/escalation work routed to a named seat is invisible to that seat's own hook loop;
  on our city the mayor seat's routed queue went undiscovered until manual checks, and two
  doctor-degraded episodes (09-04/05) were direct consequences.
- Cities that route work to named seats (mayor, deacon, review seats) get silent stalls
  that look like "no work exists" from every vantage point the affected seat itself has.
- Local mitigations in use, neither sufficient: (1) a per-agent `work_query` override so
  pool workers do not claim the routed beads meant for the named seat, and (2) explicit
  manual discovery checks on the mayor seat after every dog escalation.

## Ask

1. Confirm the ac8f6c6c `namedSelfTargetAdmit` gate is the intended fix for this scenario
   (persistent named session, self-routed frontier bead) or point us at the tracking issue
   if a piece is still open.
2. Ship it in the next tagged release so brew bottle installs stop hiding self-routed work
   from persistent named sessions. (Happy to add a repro script or additional production
   data if useful.)

title: bug: gc hook --claim re-serves dispatch-held beads (hold:mayor/hold:external) to idle workers — park/reclaim churn (v1.4.1; fix believed shipped in #6255, unreleased)
body:
# Upstream report — `gc hook --claim` re-serves dispatch-held beads (`hold:mayor`/`hold:external`) to idle workers — park/reclaim churn

**Filed:** 2026-09-16 by BeauBoorman on behalf of our fleet's city workers. Internal bead: ci-ffvu (with owner ruling authorizing upstream filing after adversarial review — review verdict: APPROVE, 2026-09-16). Sibling report: persistent-session origin gate (filed same day, same fix commit).

## Title

```
bug: gc hook --claim re-serves dispatch-held beads (hold:mayor/hold:external) to idle workers — park/reclaim churn (v1.4.1; fix believed shipped in #6255, unreleased)
```

## Summary

On gc 1.4.1 (Homebrew), a bead parked on a canonical dispatch hold (`hold:mayor` or
`hold:external`) — meaning "the required next actor is a human, not any session" — keeps
coming back through `gc hook --claim` to idle pool workers. The worker correctly re-parks
it; the next idle worker re-claims it; the loop repeats indefinitely. We witnessed one bead
take 4 idle-claim wakes across 2026-09-13→14, and the pattern was first logged 2026-09-06.
The claim frontier (both the existing-assignment serve path and the routed pool-demand
tier) keys on status+assignee and never consults the hold dimension, so the documented-correct
action (park on a hold label) re-enrolls the bead into the worker frontier forever.

This is not a local config error: the hold-blindness is embedded in the shipped binary, and
upstream tests introduced with ac8f6c6c (PR #6255) describe the same defect as their own
discovery (gas-kg6) and fix it. We are filing to (1) contribute production validation from a
bottle install, and (2) ask that the fix reach a release — no tag contains it and the brew
stable formula still ships 1.4.1.

## Environment

- macOS 27.0 (arm64); gc 1.4.1 via Homebrew (`/opt/homebrew/Cellar/gascity/1.4.1`)
- 10-rig city, one managed Dolt sql-server serving 10 rig databases + hq
- Beads provider pinned 1.2.2 (in-process store)
- Pattern reproduced across independent worker sessions on 09-06, 09-13, 09-14 (×2)

## Reproduction

1. As a worker session, park a bead that carries the `hold:mayor` (or `hold:external`)
   label: status → open (or leave in_progress), unassign, evidence documented in the bead.
2. Let any other pool worker session go idle and run `gc hook <agent> --claim --json`.
3. The held bead is returned as `action=work` and claimed (status → in_progress,
   assignee → that worker), even though its hold label marks it un-actionable by any
   machine actor.
4. The worker reads the bead, re-parks it (status → open, unassign, hold label intact).
   The next idle worker repeats from step 2. Observed 4 consecutive wakes on one bead
   over ~24 h, each burning a full worker session on re-verification before re-parking.

## Root cause (source + binary evidence, v1.4.1)

- The hook's claim path has no hold-label dimension: the existing-assignment serve path
  keys on status+assignee, and the routed pool-demand tier issues
  `bd ready --metadata-field gc.routed_to=<target> --unassigned …` with no
  `--exclude-label` for hold labels. A held bead satisfies both filters.
- Binary check of the installed 1.4.1 bottle: `strings` finds zero occurrences of
  `DispatchHoldLabels`, `PoolDemandServeRules`, or `heldLabelCountJQ`; `hold:mayor` /
  `hold:external` appear only as label data, and `--exclude-label` appears only in the bd
  flag-list string table. The shipped hook genuinely has no hold exclusion to configure.

## Upstream status (why we believe this is already fixed on main)

Commit ac8f6c6c (PR #6255, merged 2026-09-12) introduces exactly the missing dimension:

- `internal/beadmeta/hold_labels.go`: canonical `DispatchHoldLabels = {hold:mayor,
  hold:external}`.
- `internal/config/workquery.go`: `PoolDemandServeRules.ExcludeLabels` renders
  `--exclude-label hold:mayor --exclude-label hold:external` into the routed pool-demand
  tier; the in-progress serve gate counts held labels (`heldLabelCountJQ`) fail-open.
- Regression coverage: `cmd/gc/cmd_hook_claim_hold_label_test.go` pins "an in_progress
  bead assigned to this session and parked hold:external must not come back as
  action=work" (comment cites gas-kg6 — the maintainer city hit the same jam), plus
  `internal/config/workquery_inprogress_hold_test.go` for the shell tier.

**Release gap:** `git tag --contains ac8f6c6c` is empty; latest release is v1.4.1
(2026-08-15, predates the fix); Homebrew `gascity` stable = 1.4.1 (bottled). The rolling
`edge` tag is a moving main pointer, not a consumption release for bottle installs.

## Impact

- Every idle worker wake that claims a held bead wastes a full session (read bead →
  verify it is human-gated → re-park), and under pool pressure these re-claims displace
  real executable work.
- Worse than waste: a worker that does not fully re-verify risks "completing" work that
  awaits a human ruling. We treat that as the failure that made this worth reporting.
- Local mitigation in use: a per-agent `work_query` override whose pool tier appends
  `--exclude-type=chore --exclude-type=session --exclude-type=convoy
  --exclude-type=decision --exclude-label hold:mayor`, plus manual park discipline. This
  protects the discovery tier but not the existing-assignment serve path, which is why the
  release matters.

## Ask

1. Confirm the ac8f6c6c hold-label coverage is complete for the claim path (existing
   assignment serve + pool-demand tier) or point us at the tracking issue if a piece is
   still open.
2. Ship it in the next tagged release so brew bottle installs stop re-serving held beads.
   (Happy to add a repro script or additional production data if useful.)

title: fix(dolt): reclaim leaked backup archives with Dolt's native prune
body:
## Problem

A `dolt backup sync` killed after it uploads a table file but before it commits the manifest leaves that file behind, unreferenced and never reused. `examples/bd/dolt/assets/scripts/mol-dog-backup.sh` passes no prune flag, so those orphans accumulate without bound, and a larger destination makes the next sync slower, which makes the next kill more likely.

Measured on one city's `hq` backup:

| set | archives | bytes |
|---|---|---|
| referenced by the manifest | 40 | 831,295,308 |
| unreferenced (orphans) | 19 | 17,918,002,352 |

95 percent of the backup is unreachable from its own root hash. Seventeen of the 19 orphans were created on one day, in two clusters minutes apart, each about 1.08 GB.

## Fix

`dolt backup sync --prune-with-grace-period <duration>` reclaims them before uploading. It deletes only table files no manifest references, and it deletes nothing at all if any file in the destination changed inside the grace period, so a concurrent writer cannot lose data to it.

- Default `1h`: Dolt's documented choice, above its 10m floor and below the 6h sync interval in `orders/mol-dog-backup.toml`. Both bounds matter: too short and the prune runs while a writer works, too long and the previous sync's own files veto every prune.
- `GC_DOLT_BACKUP_PRUNE_GRACE` overrides it; `off` disables it. A malformed value falls back to `1h` rather than failing every backup.
- `prune_flag_for` attaches the flag per database, and only when dolt is at least 2.3.0 and that database's backup URL is `file://`. Passing the flag to an older dolt or a cloud backup fails the sync outright.
- The prune runs inside the same `dolt backup sync` invocation the existing `flock` already wraps, so it inherits that mutual exclusion.

The CHANGELOG entry for gascity#4823 and the `runtime_bounded_test.go` package comment both call the leak permanent and state that dolt has no prune verb. Dolt added the flag on 2026-08-13, so both are corrected.

This changes no timeout: raising the per-sync bound is separate work.

## Verification

Dolt 2.3.1. Run against a clone of a real 17.92 GB backup and a clone of its database, with the live copies untouched.

1. The script's own code path emitted the flag and completed:

       ++ sync_prune_flag=--prune-with-grace-period=1h
       ++ run_bounded 120 dolt backup sync --prune-with-grace-period=1h hq-backup
       backup: backup — synced: 1/1, offsite: skipped

2. Bytes actually reclaimed, not an exit code: 61 files / 18,749,299,302 bytes before, 43 files / 833,774,831 bytes after, so **17,915,524,471 bytes reclaimed**.

3. A restore from the pruned backup (`dolt backup restore file://… hq_restored_pruned`, 8.1s) matches the live store at the backup's boundary commit `m7717vrp` on full ordered scans, not counts alone:

       pruned-restore issues       rows=5420   hash=ed249b8b279ed115
       live-at-m7717vrp  issues    rows=5420   hash=ed249b8b279ed115
       pruned-restore dependencies rows=1010   hash=c30a8a63ecaf72b0
       live-at-m7717vrp  dependencies rows=1010 hash=c30a8a63ecaf72b0
       pruned-restore labels       rows=9412   hash=d793672e929f242f
       live-at-m7717vrp  labels     rows=9412  hash=d793672e929f242f

   Branch and HEAD hash match, 281 commits stay reachable, historical commits still read (`issues=5410` as of a commit 140 back), and `dolt diff --summary <root> main` walks the whole chain.

4. The idle-destination veto is real, not theoretical: an earlier attempt against a destination written two minutes before deleted nothing. Dolt also ignores files whose names are not table-file hashes, so only real archives are candidates.

`go test ./examples/bd/dolt/` fails to build in this environment for an unrelated reason (a cgo `unicode/regex.h` / icu4c header), identically on unmodified `main`. This change touches only a comment in that package.

title: feat(pricing): add the Claude 5 family to the shipped defaults
body:
## Summary

`internal/pricing/defaults.go` stops at the 4.x family (newest `last_verified`
2026-05-28). Every invocation on `claude-opus-5`, `claude-sonnet-5`,
`claude-fable-5` and `claude-fable-5-1` is therefore recorded `unpriced`, and
`gc costs` excludes unpriced invocations from `EST_USD`.

On a city that runs Opus 5 as its default work tier, that is effectively the
entire bill. In a 20-day sample from one such city, **134,962 of 135,022 model
invocations were unpriced — 0.04% coverage — and no `claude-opus-5` invocation
had ever carried a cost estimate.** `gc costs` reported a total near zero while
actual spend was in the thousands of dollars. The failure is silent in both
directions: there is no warning that a model has no rate card, and a zero
estimate is indistinguishable from "this was free".

This adds the four current Claude 5 models. Rates are Anthropic list prices
verified 2026-09-15; cache-creation uses the 5-minute (1.25x prompt) tier,
matching the existing entries.

### One entry does not follow the family convention

Claude Fable 5.1 publishes cache reads at **$0.25/MTok against a $10.00 prompt
rate** — a ratio of 40, where the rest of the family sits at 10.

That trips `TestDefaultPricingsCacheReadIsCheaperThanPrompt`, which asserted a
5–20 band:

```
default claude/claude-fable-5-1 prompt/cache-read ratio = 40.00
```

The regression that test exists to catch is *conflating* the prompt and
cache-read tiers (a ratio near 1), so the tight lower bound stays and only the
upper bound moves, to 50, with a comment recording why. Flagging it for anyone
maintaining this table: the 0.1x cache-read relationship is a convention rather
than a rule, and applying it here would have silently written $1.00.

Operators can already override any of this via `[[pricing]]` in `city.toml` or
`pack.toml`; these defaults only set the out-of-the-box behaviour.

## Testing

- [ ] `make check` — started, but the full-suite run exceeded the window I had
  to open this. I would rather show exactly what I did verify than tick a box I
  did not complete:
  - `go test ./internal/pricing/...` — ok
  - `go test ./internal/config/...` — ok (11.7s)
  - `go test ./internal/worker/...` — ok (5.4s)
  - `go vet ./...` — clean (pre-commit hook)
  - lint on `./internal/pricing` — 0 issues (pre-commit hook)
